title: Role of the Group B streptococcal Type VII Secretion System in the Diabetic Wound
text:
Diabetic wound infections are commonly colonized with pathogenic bacteria such as Group B Streptococcus
(GBS), Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterococcus faecalis, which leads to prolonged
wound healing and poor patient outcomes. However, the mechanisms by which bacteria like GBS persist and
interact with other microbes in this polymicrobial niche are not known. This proposal seeks to investigate the role
of the newly described GBS Type VII secretion system (T7SS) and its toxic secreted substrates in promoting
interbacterial competition as well as virulence in the diabetic wound.

title: Improving computational detection and genotyping of copy number variants in small complex genomes: application to high-throughput sequencing in the parasite Plasmodium falciparum
text:
The P. falciparum malaria genome is known to be highly plastic, and copy number variation has been
recognized as a driver of resistance to current and former antimalarials. This proposal aims to fill an unmet
need for accurate computational tools to survey copy number variation and its contribution to emerging drug
resistance in P. falciparum parasites from rapidly growing datasets of high-throughput whole genome and
targeted sequencing. It will also provide career development for a promising MD-PhD student as he develops
expertise in human and parasite population genomics and statistical modeling.

title: Novel Adjunctive Therapies for Pompe Disease
text:
Pompe disease is a devastating disease that affects the heart, muscles, and breathing,
particularly in infants. In this project we will use a Pompe disease mouse model to test how novel
therapies are able to clear the accumulated glycogen which is a classic sign of this disease. Once
glycogen is cleared, we will analyze the organelles responsible for nutrient recycling, which become
nonfunctional and lead to breathing problems caused by neural and muscle weakness in Pompe
disease.

title: Modulation of Acute Lung Injury by Type I Interferon Signaling
text:
Type I interferon signaling is an important host defense response to viral pathogens, but its persistent
activation at late stages of infection can paradoxically worsen lung disease. This proposal seeks to establish
the underlying molecular basis for this effect, with the long-term goal of developing new treatments for COVID-
19 and other causes of acute lung injury.

title: Nanoscale programming of celluar and physiological phenotypes
text:
We plan to continue developing a radically new technology for molecular computation, whereby molecules
themselves respond to external stimuli and produce output at the level of cellular phenotype, serving as
nanocomputing agents (NCAs). The advent of such NCAs would revolutionize the interrogation of biological
systems, enable a deeper understanding of human biology and disease, and facilitate the development of in
situ precision therapeutics.

title: Mentoring Biomechanics Research in Osteoarthritis
text:
Multidisciplinary teams investigating a multifactorial disease process like osteoarthritis is a logical and necessary
approach for innovative break-throughs in clinical practice. This award will allow the PI to expand his mentoring
of young researchers, junior faculty, postdocs, and PhD students in lower extremity biomechanics and leverage
the rich clinical environment at UCSF to open new inroads in clinical research.

title: Deciphering the immunologic landscape of Chagas cardiomyopathy pathogenesis
text:
Chagas disease is responsible for a considerable number of cases of cardiomyopathy, heart failure, and sudden
cardiac death in the Latin American population. This work aims to better understand the mechanisms that
mediate the progression towards these cardiac manifestations of disease that occur in 20-30% of individuals
infected with the causal parasite. This project will focus on investigating the spatiotemporal alterations in the
immune response that are associated with cardiac damage and will evaluate the therapeutic value of depleting
B cells in a murine model of disease.

title: SV2A PET in Spinal Cord Injury Imaging
text:
Current diagnosis of spinal cord injury (SCI) mainly relies on X-ray, CT, and
MRI, and lacks a quantitative method to evaluate the disease severity and to predict the disease projection. This
project is to develop a sensitive, reliable, and quantitative PET imaging method for the diagnosis and prognosis
of SCI. It will also allow for the noninvasive longitudinal tracking of SCI recovery and progression and guiding
the choice of the therapeutics and the assessment of the effects in clinical trials of disease-modifying
interventions.

title: hAAT-engineered Mesenchymal Stem Cells for the Treatment of Chronic Pain
text:
The overall objective of this study further explores the mechanism of protection of a novel stem cell therapy in
a pre-clinical rodent model of painful chronic pancreatitis in pain relief and inflammation reduction and
explores their potential translation to human therapy. Exploring novel strategies to reduce chronic pain is vital
for veterans’ health and VA healthcare.

title: Consequences of mast cell activation and complement dysregulation in eosinophilic esophagitis
text:
Eosinophils accumulate in the esophagus in eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE), a disease that can lead to
dysphagia and food impaction and were thought to be key cells in EoE-associated allergic inflammation;
however, recent clinical trials suggest that eosinophils are unlikely to be the primary driver of the disease. One
alternative driver of disease is mast cells, which are also elevated in the esophagus of individuals with EoE.
Our data provide compelling evidence that mast cells may be involved in disease pathogenesis, and
uncovering their role could lead to new treatments.

title: Single-Cell Epigenomics, Transcriptomics, and Bioinformatics Core
text: The PCEN at UVA will support a combined biomedical research core to assist investigators in two important areas: 1) Transcriptome and epigenome technologies and 2) Bioinformatics. The Single Cell Epigenomics, Transcriptomics, and Bioinformatics core will be directed by experienced researchers (Silvia Medrano, Ph.D. and Nathan Sheffield, Ph.D.) and staffed with highly trained personnel. Through the Single Cell Epigenomics and Transcriptomics component of the core, the PCEN will generate new data that will require substantial single cell and bioinformatics resources and expertise. The Bioinformatics component of the core will work closely with the single cell component and provide both computational infrastructure and analytical support to ensure that the investigators convert this important data into knowledge. By integrating all these services within a single core, we will ensure that PCEN investigators carry out their research in a coordinated, cost-effective, and efficient manner. The core will serve as a resource for the two PCEN main Research Projects and Pilot Projects at all times. Furthermore, the core will support the broader pediatric kidney research community at UVA and other institutions. In addition to offering a variety of specialized, innovative and essential research services, techniques, and instrumentation, the core will provide hands-on training to students, postdocs, fellows and young scientists as well as consultation services and access to state-of-the-art research equipment. Moreover, the core will provide support for preparation of manuscripts and grant proposals. The scope of the core is well in line with the overall theme of this PCEN that is “Regulation of cell fate during kidney development and disease”. The experimental approaches of the PCEN involve examination of epigenetic and transcriptional mechanisms that control cell fate, plasticity, and identity and the cellular signals underlying the phenotypic transformation that occurs during kidney injury and repair. The proposed core will provide the specialized technologies and expertise needed to accomplish the stated goals of the PCEN.

title: A physiologically relevant pre-clinical drug screening platform for Alzheimer's Disease and Traumatic Brain Injury with integrated stretchable microelectrodes
text:
Alzheimer’s Disease and related dementias are a large and growing health problem that currently affects 5.8
million Americans. Despite numerous clinical trials, there is no treatment that stops or reverses the disease
progression. This work aims to develop an efficient and physiologically relevant pre-clinical drug screening model
for Alzheimer’s Disease with the ultimate goal to develop effective treatments.

title: Molecular Mechanisms of Staphylococcus Epidermidis Strain Diversity
text:
TO PUBLIC HEALTH
Staphylococcus epidermidis is a bacteria that broadly inhabits healthy human skin, yet it is also a common
cause of skin infections and bloodstream infections associated with implanted medical devices. Because
human skin has many different types of S. epidermidis, each containing different genes, our goal is to
determine how these different genes allow S. epidermidis to switch from healthy growth in the skin to being an
infectious pathogen. Understanding this switch is critical to developing new strategies to prevent and treat
infections from S. epidermidis.

title: Tumor and host immune signatures associated with patient outcomes to GD2 chemoimmunotherapy in neuroblastoma
text: Neuroblastoma is a life-threatening childhood cancer with limited long-term survival for patients with high-risk disease. This project will identify biological and immune-related factors that influence response to current immunotherapy, with the goal of improving treatment strategies and outcomes. Insights from this study may lead to more effective, personalized approaches that reduce toxicity and increase survival in children with neuroblastoma.

title: Calcineurin signaling cascades governing Cryptococcus virulence
text:
The goal of this proposal is to elucidate calcineurin-signaling cascades governing stress responses and
virulence of the human fungal pathogen Cryptococcus, which has a significant global public health impact and
infects both immunocompromised (HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients, and others) and immunocompetent
individuals to cause life-threatening diseases of the lungs and brain (pneumonia, meningoencephalitis).
Combined, Cryptococcus species are responsible for >220,000 infections each year and more than 181,000
deaths worldwide, resulting in >15% of all HIV/AIDS-associated deaths. The studies proposed will 1) identify
and characterize novel calcineurin-interacting proteins and study these as short- and long-term effectors of
stress-responsive virulence pathways, and 2) define the roles of calcineurin re-localization to P-bodies/stress
granules during stress in operating a bifurcated stress-response pathway required for pathogenesis.

title: The UCLA Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine Scientist Training Program (PCCM-STP)
text:
Diseases related to pulmonary and critical care medicine (PCCM) remain among the leading causes of morbidity
and mortality. The UCLA Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine Scientist Training Program (PCCM-STP) is
dedicated to mentored, interdisciplinary team-based training of a new generation of academic and industry
leaders in basic, clinical translational and health services research. By deploying facilities and resources of
renowned multidisciplinary mentor faculty, we will fulfill the program mission of training a cadre of investigators
who will discover novel underlying basic principles of PCCM-related diseases and translate these discoveries to
improve health.

title: Tau variants in FUS-mediated ALS
text:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a complex neurodegenerative disease with approximately 10-15%
familial cases that are caused by genetic mutations largely in an autosomal dominant fashion. In an extended
ALS kindred carrying an ALS-linked mutation in the Fused in Sarcoma (FUS) gene, we discovered that a
subset of individuals carrying the FUS mutation remained free from ALS even beyond their 60s (unaffected
mutation carriers, UMCs), and we identified a cluster of linked variants in the 3’ untranslated region of the
MAPT gene in UMCs as a putative protective modifier. We propose to use patient-derived induced pluripotent
stem cells (iPSC) and their differentiated motor neurons (iMNs) as well as isogenic lines with or without the
MAPT variants to test the hypothesis that the MAPT variants reduce Tau protein expression, mitigate iMN
hyperexcitability, and protect UMCs from developing ALS.

title: Investigation of hepatic factor in pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
text:
The goal of this project is to improve our understanding of pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs),
which are common sequelae of surgical palliation for univentricular congenital heart disease. To achieve this
goal, we will study a circulating protein (soluble vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 1; sVEGFR1),
which we recently identified as a candidate factor that may prevent PAVMs. By studying the role of sVEGFR1
in vascular remodeling and PAVM prevention, we anticipate that this new knowledge will improve our
understanding of pulmonary microvascular biology and may lead to development of targeted medical therapies
for patients with univentricular congenital heart disease and PAVMs.

title: The Louisiana Clinical Center of Nutrition for Precision Health (LA-NPH)
text:
The Louisiana Nutrition for Precision Health Center (LA-NPH), consisting of LSU-Pennington Biomedical in Baton Rouge and LSU-Health Sciences Center in New Orleans aims to recruit participants from the All of Us research program into the three proposed modules of the NPH consortium. In Module 1 (n=900), we will carefully catalogue habitual dietary intake and measure the response to a standard mixed meal
tolerance test (MMTT) and collect baseline measures of health, behavior and environment. In Module 2 (n=145) and Module 3 (n=60) the inter-individual variability to three distinct eucaloric diets, each eaten for 2-weeks in a crossover randomized order will be assessed in free-living and domiciled individuals, respectively.

title: Defining and exploiting therapeutically the role of nociceptor neuron–tumor–pericyte axis that drives melanoma progression via CGRP-RAMP1 signaling
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health as it focuses on the discovery of a novel signaling pathway
involved in the regulation of melanoma metastases by the nervous system. The goal of this study is to determine
the mechanisms by which nociceptor signaling via RAMP1 (receptor activity modifying protein 1) in malignant
cells and pericytes regulates melanoma metastases and the relevance of RAMP1 expression in the outcomes
of patients with metastatic melanoma. We will use human metastatic melanoma specimens and clinically relevant
metastatic melanoma mouse models in combination with genetic state-of-the-art technologies to reveal novel
pathways for the mechanistic and therapeutic significance of nociceptor neurons’ role via RAMP1 signaling in
metastatic melanoma.
